fact.zermelo: Zermelo proved in 1913 that in every finite two-player game of perfect information without chance, either one player can force a win or both can force a draw. Nobody knows which for chess.
fact.hex_draw: Hex can never end in a draw, and John Nash showed that the first player must win with perfect play — by a strategy-stealing argument that proves a winning strategy exists without saying what it is.
fact.hex_invented: Piet Hein invented Hex in 1942, and John Nash reinvented it independently in 1948.
fact.pie_rule: The pie rule — one player cuts, the other chooses which side to take — fixes a first-move advantage by making the opening move as fair as the first player can bear.
fact.nim: Charles Bouton solved the game of Nim in 1901. The Sprague–Grundy theorem later showed that every impartial game is secretly a Nim heap.
fact.rps: In rock–paper–scissors the only equilibrium strategy is to play each option a third of the time. Game designers use the same idea of a cycle to keep any one unit or faction from being best.
fact.dominant: A dominant strategy — one that is best whatever the opponent does — is usually a design bug: it removes the decision. Good strategy games make the best move depend on the position.
fact.nash: Nash's equilibrium (1950) and the prisoner's dilemma (devised the same year at RAND) are the two ideas of game theory that designers meet most often, usually without calling them that.
fact.yavalath: Yavalath was invented by a computer: Cameron Browne's LUDI program generated and play-tested thousands of rule sets in 2007. Four in a row wins — but make three first and you lose.
fact.cepheus: Games with hidden information need different mathematics: in 2015 the researchers behind Cepheus announced that heads-up limit hold'em was essentially solved by counterfactual regret minimization.
fact.elo: Elo's rating system, devised by Arpad Elo for chess and adopted by FIDE in 1970, predicts the chance of winning from the rating difference alone — which is why it also sorts players of nearly every game.
fact.branching: A game's branching factor — how many moves a player can choose from — is the design lever that decides whether computers can search it. Chess averages about 35; Go about 250.
fact.intransitive: Intransitive dice and rock–paper–scissors show that “better than” need not be transitive: A can beat B, B beat C, and C beat A. Many card and faction games rely on it.
fact.hidden_info: Chess and Go have no hidden information and no dice. Add either — poker's hidden cards, the combat dice of a war game — and a search must also weigh chances, not just replies.
fact.monte_carlo: The Monte Carlo method was invented by Stanisław Ulam in the 1940s while he was wondering how likely a game of solitaire was to come out; John von Neumann helped turn it into a program for the ENIAC computer, and Nicholas Metropolis named it after the casino.
fact.mcts: Monte Carlo tree search plays thousands of random games from a position and keeps statistics, steering toward moves that win more often. UCT (2006) added the rule for how often to try each move again.
fact.alpha_beta: Alpha-beta pruning gives the same answer as minimax while skipping moves that cannot matter. With perfect move ordering it searches about b^(d/2) positions instead of b^d: twice as deep for the same effort.
fact.minimax: Minimax comes from John von Neumann's 1928 minimax theorem: in a two-player zero-sum game, each side picks the move whose worst case is best.
fact.shannon: Claude Shannon wrote down how a computer could play chess in 1950, and estimated about 10^120 possible games — the Shannon number — far more than the roughly 10^80 atoms in the observable universe.
fact.deep_blue: Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 while searching around 200 million chess positions per second.
fact.alphago: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1 in March 2016. It combined Monte Carlo tree search with neural networks that suggested moves and judged positions, instead of relying on random playouts alone.
fact.bots: {brand}'s bots span the usual ladder: random, a tactical bot that looks for immediate wins and threats, minimax with alpha-beta, and Monte Carlo tree search.
fact.transposition: A transposition table remembers positions a search has already analysed, because the same position can be reached by different move orders. Without one, searches repeat enormous amounts of work.
fact.deepening: Iterative deepening searches one move deep, then two, then three, and so on until the clock runs out. The repeated work is a small price, because each level costs several times more than the one before.
fact.checkers_solved: Checkers was solved in 2007 — a draw with perfect play — by combining a search of the opening with databases of every endgame position, built by working backwards from the finished games.
fact.playouts: Monte Carlo playouts need no evaluation function, only the rules of the game. That is why the same search can play Hex, Tak or Fendo with no game-specific knowledge.
fact.chess_positions: There are about 4.8 × 10^44 legal positions in chess (John Tromp's 2021 estimate) — and exactly 2.08 × 10^170 legal positions on a 19×19 Go board, more than the atoms in the universe squared.
fact.tak_6x6: A 6×6 Tak board can be filled in at most about 3.7 × 10^53 ways within the pieces each player owns (30 stones and a capstone), ignoring which of them can ever occur. Chess has about 4.8 × 10^44 legal positions.
fact.tak_5x5: Tak on 5×5 can be filled in at most about 2.6 × 10^37 ways within the 21 stones and capstone each player owns, again ignoring reachability. Adding one row and one column (6×6) multiplies that by about 14 quadrillion.
fact.connect_four: Connect Four has 4,531,985,219,092 reachable positions and was solved in 1988: the first player wins with perfect play, starting in the middle column.
fact.tic_tac_toe: Tic-tac-toe has 255,168 possible games but only 5,478 different legal positions. Almost all of the games are the same few positions reached in different orders.
fact.checkers_size: Checkers has about 5 × 10^20 positions. Jonathan Schaeffer's Chinook team finished solving it in 2007: with perfect play it is a draw.
fact.rubik: A Rubik's Cube has 43 quintillion arrangements, yet any of them can be solved in at most 20 moves — “God's number”, proven in 2010 with about 35 CPU-years of idle computer time donated by Google.
fact.tak_origin: Tak is a game from Patrick Rothfuss's novel The Wise Man's Fear (2011). Rothfuss and James Ernest turned the fictional game into a real one, with stones, walls and a capstone that flattens walls.
fact.tak_stacks: In Tak a stack can be moved by the player whose stone is on top, carrying up to as many stones as the board is wide. Stacking is why Tak positions are so much more numerous than the squares suggest.
fact.ur: The Royal Game of Ur was played in Mesopotamia more than 4,000 years ago — a race game with safe rosette squares, whose rules were pieced together from a cuneiform tablet.
fact.go_age: Go is more than 2,500 years old. Its rules fit on a page; its strategy has filled libraries.
fact.havannah: Havannah, from Christian Freeling (1979), was designed to be hard for computers: the board is a hexagon of hexagons and a win may be a bridge, a fork or a ring. Freeling once offered a prize to any program that beat strong human players.

tour.welcome_text: Abstract strategy games, from classics like Go and Hex to new designs. Pick a game from the list to play it: you don't need to sign up.
tour.welcome_alt: The list of games, each with a picture of its board.
tour.opponents_text: Play a friend by sending them the game's link, or play a bot as strong as you like. You can also set two bots against each other and watch.
tour.opponents_alt: A game's setup, with the choice of opponent: a friend, yourself, a bot or two bots.

tour.learn_alt: The rules window of a game, open at its rules.
tour.table_text: Choose a piece and the places it can go light up. Build your move, go back if you change your mind, and submit it when it's right. Offer a draw, chat with the table, or talk over voice chat.
tour.table_alt: A game of Tak in play, a piece chosen and the squares it can move to marked.
tour.puzzles_text: Puzzles give you a position with a win to find. In a game, a bot can give you a hint, and afterwards you can replay it move by move and play on from any point.
tour.puzzles_alt: A puzzle: a position to win from, with a Solve button.
tour.analysis_text: Set bots playing hundreds of games of any game in the background, then read the report: how often each side wins, how the games end, and which bot is stronger.
tour.analysis_alt: A report of a batch of bot games: the win rate of each side, with a line at an even share.
tour.games_text: Your games wait for you. The games button at the top counts those where it's your turn, so you can play several at once, at your own pace.
tour.games_alt: The list of your games: one where it's your turn, one waiting for the other player, one in its lobby.
tour.compete_text: Play rated games for a rating in each game, enter tournaments, and earn badges for the moments worth telling people about.
tour.compete_alt: A table of ratings, and a badge earned.
tour.friends_text: Add friends by their handle, see who's online, write to them, call them and invite them straight into a game. And everybody meets in the global chat.
tour.friends_alt: The friends window: friends with a dot for who is online, and a conversation.
tour.muster_text: Can't all play now? Call a muster: offer the times you could play, the people you invite tick the ones they can make, and the game is set for the earliest time that suits everyone, with an invitation for their calendars.
tour.muster_alt: A muster in a game's lobby: the times offered, each with how many can make it.
tour.guest_text: Your guest key is what makes your games yours, and this browser keeps it. To play on your phone or another computer too, open your profile, the person at the top, and choose Move to Another Device.
tour.guest_alt: The Move to Another Device part of the profile window, with the button that copies your guest key.

autoplay.title: Auto-Play Timeout
autoplay.help_1: Players do not always have the time to take their turn when it comes. With the Auto-Play Timeout on, the game does not wait for you for ever: when it is your turn to act — a turn of your own, or a reaction waiting for your answer — and you have not acted within the time you set, a tactical bot takes the turn for you.
autoplay.help_2: The wait is counted from the last move in the game: the one that made it your turn, or your own last decision. Every move you make, and every move the bot makes for you, starts the count again.
autoplay.help_3: The bot plays the decisions of that turn, one after the other, until play passes to another player. Then the count starts over for your next turn.
autoplay.help_4: It is the tactical bot — the same one you can add to an empty seat: sensible, not brilliant. It will play your seat as it sees fit.
autoplay.help_5: Every move it makes for you is marked “auto-play” in the Moves tab, and the turn is marked in the History tab, so everyone can see who really played it.
autoplay.help_6: You can switch it off, or change the time, whenever you like, even while it is your turn. It is off by default; when you switch it on it starts at 24 hours.
autoplay.help_7: Dice that the bot rolled for you cannot be rolled again: you cannot take those moves back.

react.when_targeted: an action is aimed at you
react.help_1: Reactions are abilities you can use on another player's turn. Each time another player acts, the game works out whether you could react, and would then wait for you.
react.help_2: With “When I'm targeted” on (it is by default) you are asked whenever an opponent's action is aimed at you, at something of yours or at a place where you have something.
react.help_3: When you are not targeted, your reaction is passed for you and the move list shows it as an automatic pass. Switch the option off to be asked less, or add “After any other player's action” or chosen players below to be asked more.
